name: EventMemAgent

paper.title: EventMemAgent: Hierarchical Event-Centric Memory for Online Video Understanding with Adaptive Tool Use

construction.unit: video event: frames in short-term memory; first frame + caption + embedding + change log in long-term memory
construction.kept_as: raw frames (STM, reservoir-sampled) and an MLLM caption of each archived event
construction.processing: 1 fps frames; cut an event when the gray-histogram correlation with the event falls below 0.2 (after 8 frames); on eviction a 4B VLM captions the event and describes the change from the previous event

organization.structure: two tiers: short-term buffer of up to 32 frames grouped into events; long-term list of event records linked by change logs
organization.stores: STM frame buffer; LTM event list
organization.index: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B vectors of captions; event time ranges

management.operations: FIFO: when STM exceeds 32 frames the oldest event moves to LTM; a single event filling STM is thinned by reservoir sampling
management.forgetting: reservoir sampling drops frames of a long event before captioning; LTM keeps every archived event

retrieval.query: agent-written text query or time range, via tool calls
retrieval.candidates: cosine similarity of query to caption embeddings (text mode) or overlap with a time range (time mode)
retrieval.selection: top 3 events, similarity ≥ 0.3 (text mode); agent decides whether and how often to search
retrieval.budget: 3 events per search; up to 10 agent turns in the evaluation scripts

use.context: all STM frames (≤ 32, labelled with frame number and time) + returned event captions, change logs and first frames + OCR/detection outputs
use.reasoning: ReAct loop of the RL-trained agent; answer in \boxed{}

classify.note: The agent chooses when and what to search, but each search returns a fixed top 3 by similarity (or time overlap).

stages.ingestion: The stream is sampled at 1 fps; each frame is compared with the current event by the Pearson correlation of gray-level histograms and starts a new event when it falls below 0.2, once the event has at least 8 frames.
stages.construction: When an event leaves short-term memory, Qwen3-VL-4B writes a one-paragraph caption from up to 32 of its frames, the caption is embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, and a change log sentence is generated from the first frames of this and the previous event.
stages.organization: Short-term memory holds at most 32 frames grouped into events and is shown to the agent in full; long-term memory is an ordered list of event records (first frame, time range, caption, embedding, change from previous / to next).
stages.update: When the buffer is full the oldest event moves to long-term memory (FIFO); if one event alone fills it, new frames replace random ones with probability 32/n (reservoir sampling).
stages.retrieval: The agent calls search_memory with a text query (cosine to caption embeddings, top 3 with similarity ≥ 0.3) or a time range (top 3 by overlap); it can also run OCR or object detection on an event's first frame or an STM frame.
stages.answer: Qwen3-VL-8B reasons over the STM frames and tool observations in a ReAct loop and answers in \boxed{}.
stages.learning: The agent's reasoning and tool use are trained end to end with GRPO (group size 8, KL 0) on 10K MovieChat samples with a 0/1 answer-correctness reward; memory construction is not trained.

summary: Online video agent whose memory has two tiers: a 32-frame buffer segmented into events by histogram change (with reservoir sampling), and a long-term list of captioned events with change logs that an RL-trained MLLM agent searches and inspects with OCR and detection tools.
notes: Video memory, not dialogue: the 'turns' are 1 fps frames. Paper v2 (11 Sep 2026) read from the arXiv PDF; LNCS-style template, no venue stated, so recorded as a preprint. Code checked at commit 203e635b (8 Sep 2026), the release of training, inference and evaluation code. Benchmark scoring: OVO-Bench overall = mean of the three category averages (e.g. (68.29+58.03+55.92)/3 = 60.75); StreamingBench ALL is weighted accuracy per docs/EVALUATION.md.

open_questions: The fixed-length ablation (30 s segments) changes STM buffering and LTM units at once, so event segmentation and reservoir sampling are not separated.
No ablation removes long-term memory or the search tool, and StreamingBench (the paper notes) depends mostly on current frames, so the share of the gain due to memory is not measured.
The RL, tools and memory are added together: the untrained agent (56.16) is barely above the base model (55.81) on OVO-Bench overall, and the jump to 60.75 comes with training.

glance.a: An event: a run of 1 fps frames with a similar gray histogram. In short-term memory it is the frames themselves; in long-term memory it is the first frame, time range, a VLM caption with its embedding, and a change log.
Yes, when an event leaves the 32-frame buffer: a 4B VLM writes one paragraph from up to 32 of its frames. Other frames are discarded.
Two tiers: a 32-frame buffer grouped into events (FIFO, reservoir sampling within a single long event) and an ordered list of archived events linked by change logs.
No. A text search keeps the top 3 captions by cosine similarity (≥ 0.3); a time search keeps the top 3 by overlap.

glance.q: Is memory reconstructed at question time?
glance.a: The agent can search again, change the query, or run OCR and detection on stored frames, for up to 10 turns; the policy is trained with GRPO.
Always the ≤ 32 recent frames; plus whatever its searches return (caption, change logs, first frame per event) and tool outputs.

discussion.takeaway: Keep a small event-segmented frame buffer, archive older events as captioned records, and train the MLLM with RL to decide when to search them or zoom in with OCR and detection. With at most 32 frames in context it beats the other open-source models on OVO-Bench and is competitive on StreamingBench.

claims.claim: Best open-source result on OVO-Bench, above GPT-4o.
claims.evidence: 60.75 overall vs 59.54 GPT-4o and 55.81 Qwen3-VL-8B with 64 frames. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Competitive on StreamingBench real-time tasks with ≤ 32 frames.
claims.evidence: 77.00 vs 77.26 StreamForest and 75.69 Gemini 1.5 Pro. Table 2
58.27 → 60.75 on OVO-Bench and 75.09 → 77.00 on StreamingBench. Table 3
Without detection 57.80, without OCR 58.98, vs 60.75. Table 4

claims.claim: Agentic RL is needed to use memory and tools.
claims.evidence: Untrained agent 56.16 / 68.44 vs 60.75 / 77.00; Backward Tracing 46.18 (base) → 56.33 (untrained) → 58.03. Table 6, App. C

claims.claim: Latency stays flat as the video grows.
claims.evidence: Median 1.78 s up to 30 min; tools 1.6% of latency. Fig. 4, §4.3

limits: StreamingBench mostly rewards perception of current frames, so the long-term memory is not fully exercised there (stated as a caveat, §4.2).
reading: Only captions are embedded; change logs and first frames come back with a hit but never decide which events are found.
A long event is captioned from at most 32 frames that survived reservoir sampling (e.g. Event 11 in Fig. 9 spans 228-431 s from 32 frames).
The change log is written from two first frames, so it describes how the openings of consecutive events differ, not what happened within them.
Baselines use different frame budgets (64 frames or 1 fps) and the paper does not say whether their numbers were rerun or taken from earlier reports.
No row removes long-term memory while keeping the trained agent, so memory's own contribution is not isolated; the fixed-length ablation keeps a long-term memory.
Base and fine-tuned models differ in training as well as memory: EventMemAgent is Qwen3-VL-8B after GRPO on MovieChat, while the Qwen3-VL row is the untrained model.

abstract.text: EventMemAgent targets online video question answering, where an unbounded stream must fit a fixed MLLM context. It keeps a short-term buffer of recent frames split into events by visual change and thinned by reservoir sampling, and moves older events into a long-term store as captioned, searchable records with change logs. An MLLM agent searches that store and applies OCR and object detection, and its reasoning and tool use are trained end to end with GRPO. The authors report strong results on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench with at most 32 input frames.
